opus-5.5.text:
Well, "fractal intelligence" was really my attempt at an honest description, not an explanation. What I mean by it is that these systems are amazing at some things, and then you nudge the problem slightly, change the names in a blocks-world problem, obfuscate the predicates, make the plan one step longer, and the performance just falls off a cliff. Pull up any point in the capability landscape and you can't predict, from the neighboring points, whether it's going to be brilliant or embarrassing. It looks jagged at every scale. That's the fractal part.

But here's my concern. If all we ever say is "it's fractal," then we've basically given up on science. We've turned it into an anecdote collection: "look, it did this impressive thing," "look, it failed on this trivial thing." Twitter is full of both, and people pick whichever set confirms their priors. That's not a science of LLMs. That's astrology with benchmarks.

What we actually need is some characterization of *when* these things work and *why*. When I say they're approximate retrieval engines, or that they are doing a kind of universal approximate retrieval over a gigantic corpus, that's a hypothesis you can test. It predicts that performance should track something like closeness to the training distribution, rather than the intrinsic computational complexity of the problem. And in fact, that's what we keep seeing: the cost of the computation an LLM spends doesn't scale with the difficulty of the problem the way it would for a real reasoner. A sound planner takes longer on harder problems. An LLM spends the same per-token compute whether you ask it for a poem or a solution to an NP-complete problem. That tells you something about what's going on underneath.

And this matters even more now with the so-called reasoning models, the o1-style systems trained with RL on derivational traces. People say, "Oh, now they reason." Okay, maybe they're doing something more, and in some of our work we did see genuine improvements on planning. But you have to ask: what's the guarantee? What's the cost? Is the intermediate trace actually semantically meaningful, or is it just a prompt augmentation that happens to help? We've shown you can train on traces that are essentially wrong and still get improvements in final accuracy. So anthropomorphizing those tokens as "thinking" is again description masquerading as explanation.

So the reason to go beyond "fractal" is practical too. If you want to deploy these systems in anything safety-critical, you need to know in advance where the cliffs are. You can't say "it's fractal, good luck." That's why I keep pushing for things like LLM-Modulo frameworks, where the LLM generates candidates and sound external verifiers check them. That gives you guarantees in spite of the jaggedness. But the deeper scientific goal should be to characterize the shape of that fractal, not just admire it.

r001.rationale: It describes performance as jagged and unpredictable across small changes, with no reliable way to infer success from neighboring capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says research should characterize when LLMs work, why they work, and where their performance cliffs are, so their reliability can be understood before deployment.

r003.rationale: It contrasts LLM compute, which it says does not scale with problem difficulty, with a sound planner and argues performance tracks training-distribution closeness rather than intrinsic complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, "fractal intelligence" was my phrase, and I still think it's a useful description. What I meant by it is that if you probe these systems, you find they're brilliant on one problem and then you perturb it slightly, change the names, change the ordering, add an irrelevant clause, and they fall apart. And the failures don't have a clean boundary. You can't say "it's good at problems of this type and bad at problems of that type." At every scale you look, you find these pockets of competence and incompetence sitting right next to each other. That's the fractal picture.

But here's the thing. A description is not a theory. Saying "it's fractal" is like a cartographer saying the coastline is jagged. It tells you something, but it doesn't tell you why the coastline is jagged or where the next inlet will be. And right now a lot of what passes for the science of LLMs is really just this kind of ethnography. People go in, they prompt the thing, they collect anecdotes, they tweet them, and somebody says "see, it reasons," and somebody else says "see, it doesn't." That's not a science, that's a Rorschach test.

So what would it mean to go beyond? I think we have to stop asking the question "is it intelligent" and start asking "what is the computation it's actually doing." If you believe, as I do, that these are essentially very sophisticated approximate retrieval systems, that they're doing something like interpolation over an enormous training distribution, then the fractal pattern is not mysterious at all. It's exactly what you'd predict. Where the training data was dense, performance is good. Where it was sparse, it degrades. And the "density" of the training distribution is itself a very irregular object, so you get an irregular competence landscape. The fractal is a shadow cast by the data.

Now, that's a hypothesis, and the point is that it's a testable one. You can construct problems where you control the distance from the training distribution. We did this with planning, with Blocks World, with the "mystery" versions where we obfuscate the predicate names so the problem is semantically identical but lexically unfamiliar. And performance craters. That's the kind of experiment that distinguishes between "it has learned to plan" and "it has learned to pattern-match on plans it has seen." Those are different claims with different consequences, and only one of them tells you where the next inlet is going to be.

The other reason I think we need to move past the descriptive stage is a practical one. People are building things on top of these systems, agents, tool-use pipelines, systems that are supposed to act in the world. And if your only scientific understanding is "its capabilities are fractal," you have no principled way to say when it will fail. You're just hoping. Whereas if you understand it as a generator of plausible completions that needs to be paired with a verifier, a sound external check, then you have an architecture, what I call the LLM-Modulo framework, where you get the generative breadth of the model without having to trust its correctness. That only follows from having a model of what the thing is, not just a description of how it behaves.

So I'd say "fractal intelligence" was a good first observation. It killed the naive story that these systems are either fully reasoning or fully parroting. But a good observation should be the beginning of a research program, not the end of one. We owe it to ourselves to actually explain the fractal, not just admire it.

r001.rationale: The response says fractal competence has no clean boundaries and that the description alone gives no principled way to know when a system will fail.

r002.rationale: It calls for a testable account of the computation and explains that understanding it would help predict failures and determine when outputs need external verification.

r003.rationale: The response critiques anecdotal evaluations and the reasoning-versus-parroting dichotomy, but does not say that existing formal characterizations of reasoning limits fail to fit LLMs.

astra-6.text:
Well, calling it “fractal intelligence” may capture our surprise, but it doesn’t explain the phenomenon. You look at one task and the model seems extraordinarily capable; you look at a closely related task and it fails. Giving that unevenness a name is a starting point. The scientific question is whether we can predict where those successes and failures will occur.

For example, if a model solves a planning problem, what have we established? Can it reliably handle variations of that problem? Can it recognize when its proposed plan violates a constraint? Can it correct the plan? Those are distinct capabilities, and a convincing answer to one instance doesn’t establish all of them.

We need hypotheses that can be tested and potentially falsified. What aspects of performance come from familiarity with the task? What generalizes when we change the structure? What happens as the problem gets harder? If every success and every failure is equally compatible with “fractal intelligence,” then the phrase gives us very little explanatory purchase.

And this matters practically. If we want to build systems people can depend on, we need to understand when the model’s suggestions require verification and what can provide that verification. The remarkable capabilities are precisely why we should demand a more precise science of them.

r001.rationale: The response says performance varies across closely related tasks and asks whether science can predict where successes and failures occur, conveying uncertainty about when LLMs will succeed.

r002.rationale: It asks whether results hold across variations and says we need to understand when suggestions require verification, addressing how far results can be relied upon.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss existing formal characterizations of reasoning limits or say that they fail to fit LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, calling it “fractal intelligence” captures the impression that these systems can be remarkably good at one thing and surprisingly bad at something that looks very similar. But that is the phenomenon we need to explain. Giving it a name doesn’t yet give us a scientific account of it.

We need to ask: under what conditions does a capability hold? What changes make it fail? Can we predict those failures before we see them? If every success is evidence of intelligence and every failure is another wrinkle in the fractal, then what observation would make us revise our explanation?

Take planning. Producing something that looks like a plan is different from producing a plan whose actions actually achieve the goal. We can check that distinction against explicit constraints. And if the model fails, we can investigate whether it misunderstood the task, missed a constraint, or simply generated a plausible sequence without establishing that it works.

The point isn’t to deny that these systems are impressive. It’s to turn that surprise into testable claims. A scientific understanding should help us predict when to trust the system, when to verify its output, and what additional machinery it needs.

r001.rationale: It describes systems as succeeding remarkably at some things and failing at similar ones, then asks when capabilities hold and what changes make them fail.

r002.rationale: It says scientific understanding should predict when to trust the system and when to verify its output, directly addressing how far results can be relied upon.

r003.rationale: It discusses testable explanations and planning checks, but does not state that existing formal characterizations of reasoning limits fail to fit LLMs.
